key_features.classic_presentation: GERD presents with burning substernal or epigastric discomfort (heartburn), regurgitation of acid, worse when lying down or bending over. Chronic/recurrent pattern. May have chronic cough or hoarseness.
key_features.typical_demographics: Affects 20% of adults. Risk factors: obesity, hiatal hernia, pregnancy, smoking. Can occur at any age.
key_features.pathophysiology_brief: Lower esophageal sphincter dysfunction allows gastric acid to reflux into esophagus, causing mucosal irritation.

diagnostic_questions.context: Burning quality is hallmark. Substernal or epigastric location.
Supine position worsens reflux. Patients often sleep with head elevated.
GERD is chronic condition with episodic symptoms, not acute first presentation.
Regurgitation of acid or food is specific for GERD.
Response to antacids/PPIs is supportive of GERD diagnosis.

differential_diagnosis.key_difference: Pressure/heaviness, exertional, radiation to arm/jaw, no positional change

red_flags.action: Possible stricture or malignancy - needs endoscopy
Concerning for malignancy - urgent evaluation needed

typical_management: Lifestyle modifications: elevate head of bed, avoid triggers (alcohol, caffeine, spicy foods), weight loss. PPI therapy (omeprazole, pantoprazole). Most respond well to treatment.
disposition: Outpatient management. Endoscopy if alarm symptoms or refractory to treatment.
patient_education: GERD is chronic acid reflux that can damage the esophagus. Treatment includes lifestyle changes and medications to reduce acid. Most people get good relief with PPIs.
